title: The old man's horse
hookLine: a lost horse, a found herd, a broken leg, a son spared from war: who can say what is lucky? (Huainanzi 18)

lines: THE JOB GOES TO SOMEONE ELSE.
THE OLD MAN'S HORSE RUNS AWAY.
cards: The job offer goes to someone else. Three months later, the company folds. The dream apartment comes through, and the upstairs neighbor turns out to play drums at midnight.
Bad news that turns out good, good news that turns out hard: it's an old pattern, and easy to forget each time the next piece of news arrives. An old Chinese story tells of a man who doesn't forget.
He lives near the frontier, where China meets the lands of the northern horse peoples. And one day, his horse runs away.

teach.b: The horse gallops off across the border and is gone. The neighbors come to say how sorry they are. The old man says: how do you know this isn't a blessing?

teach.h: IT COMES BACK WITH A HERD.
teach.b: Months later, the horse comes home, bringing a herd of fine horses from the north. The neighbors come to congratulate him. How do you know this isn't a disaster?
His son loves the new horses, rides them, and one day falls and breaks his leg badly. He'll limp for life. The neighbors are sorry again.
How do you know this isn't a blessing? A year later, raiders cross the border. Every able-bodied young man is called up to fight, and nine in ten of the men from the frontier die.

teach.h: THE SON STAYS HOME FROM WAR.
teach.b: The son, because of his leg, stays home. Father and son both live. The story comes from a Chinese book called the Huainanzi, put together at a prince's court and drawing heavily on Taoist ideas.
Today it lives on as a Chinese saying for when something goes wrong: the old man at the frontier lost his horse. Some modern retellings give the old man one word: maybe. Good luck?
The old book puts it as a question, how do you know, but the heart is the same. It's tempting to judge every event the instant it happens, as if the story were over. It never is.
The old man isn't cold, and he isn't saying nothing matters. He just refuses to close the book on page one.

how: In China the saying "the old man at the frontier lost his horse" is used to comfort someone after a setback, and the story is retold in Taoist and self-help settings, sometimes with the old man's answer shortened to "maybe".

games.q: you're the old man. your runaway horse has come home leading a herd of fine horses. the neighbors congratulate you. what do you say?

I knew it would come back.
games.why: he asks how they know it isn't a disaster, and soon his son falls from one of the new horses. then that turns out to save his life.

practice: Breathe out slowly, then find something from this week that got its label, good or bad, the moment it happened. Run the story forward the way the neighbors never did: and then what? And then?
At each new turn, say maybe; don't force it to be secretly good, just leave the story open past page one.

wordCard.voice: Huainanzi. The old Chinese book that tells of a lost horse, a found herd, a broken leg, and a life spared, each time met with: how do you know?

orig.note: Chinese, sài wēng shī mǎ: the old man at the frontier lost his horse, a four-word saying from this story.

carryVoice: Your line: maybe. The horse may still come back over the border. That's day fifty-five.
